title: Species intraspecific variation drives tropical forest drought resistance.

verified.what_i_actually_checked: Dryad API metadata for doi:10.5061/dryad.r4xgxd2vb (version 457112): five files, total 112,792 bytes. The one data table is PueroRicoHydraulicTraitData.csv at 38,245 bytes; the rest are three R scripts and a README. Both file-download routes (API /files/<id>/download and the web file_stream link) returned 401/403 to automated requests, so I never saw the rows or columns.
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: 290 trees, 18 species, 11 hydraulic traits, Puerto Rico rainfall gradient of 1,000 to 4,000 mm per year, all from the abstract (no open full text; Europe PMC has no PMCID). A 38 KB file fits roughly 290 rows by about 15 to 20 numeric columns, but I did not count the rows myself.

a1_downloadable.note: Public Dryad dataset with no access application. Automated download was blocked (401/403), but a person in a browser should be able to get it. Only the file listing was verified.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: Not verified in the files. Hydraulic traits such as P50 (the water potential at which a stem loses 50% of its conductivity) would each be a measured column per tree, according to the abstract.

a3_inputs_present.note: Not verified. The likely inputs (site rainfall, species, the other traits) would be columns in the same CSV.

a4_units_stated.note: Not verified. The README (3,238 bytes) probably documents the units, but I couldn't download it.

a5_enough_rows.note: The paper reports 290 trees, and the 38,245-byte CSV size fits that. That is far below the ~1,500-row bar for regression and below 400 even for classification. Row count not counted from the file.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: Not checkable without the file. The file size is consistent with 290 rows.

a8_label_provenance.note: Per the paper, the traits are physical measurements on field-collected branches (embolism resistance, stomatal closure), not model outputs.

backbone.name: none (tabular plant-trait data; no pretrained backbone fits)
backbone.licence: Dryad datasets are CC0 (public domain dedication)

integration.partner_dataset: TRY plant trait database or the Xylem Functional Traits database (global P50 compilations), joinable on species name
integration.bigger_question_one_sentence: Does within-species variation in drought resistance along one island's rainfall gradient match the pattern across species worldwide?

controls.positive_control: P50 should become more negative (more embolism-resistant) at drier sites, which is the paper's headline result.
controls.external_validation: Global trait compilations (Xylem Functional Traits database), but those are mostly per-species means, not per-tree values.

honest_claim_h3: Among 290 trees of 18 species sampled at a few sites on one Caribbean island, how hydraulic traits change with mean annual rainfall within and between species. That is a mixed-effects statistics question, not an ML one.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use a tree's species and the rainfall at its site to predict how resistant its water-transport tissue is to drought damage.
plain_idea.train_on: One row per tree: species, site rainfall and the other measured hydraulic traits. About 290 trees, according to the paper; I couldn't count them in the file.
plain_idea.predict: Embolism resistance (how much water stress a branch can take before air bubbles block half its water-transport vessels), measured on field-collected branches.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: Forest drought models usually give every species one fixed trait value, so a per-tree predictor could improve forecasts. But 290 trees across 18 species is too few for ML; the paper's mixed-effects regression is the right tool.

ml_idea: Predict per-tree P50 (embolism resistance) from species, site rainfall and the other traits, holding out whole sites. With about 290 rows, this cannot beat or add to the paper's Bayesian mixed models.

effort.compute_note: Estimated from the 38 KB file size; nothing timed.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Count the rows of PueroRicoHydraulicTraitData.csv. The paper says 290 trees, which already fails A5.

verdict_reason: Fails A5 (too few rows). The only data table is a 38 KB CSV covering 290 trees of 18 species (paper count, consistent with the file size), far below the 1,500-row regression bar or 400-row classification bar. Automated download from Dryad was also blocked, so I never opened the columns.
